one_liner: Header-only C++17 Flask-style HTTP/WebSocket framework on Asio; a 2014 first-party /json run beat Go net/http by ~1.5x.
what_it_does: Crow is a C++ web framework for HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket services, with Flask-like route macros (CROW_ROUTE(app, "/hello/<int>")) whose handler argument types are checked at compile time. It includes a JSON reader/writer (crow::json), Mustache templating, middleware (CORS, cookies, sessions), multipart parsing, optional HTTPS (OpenSSL) and gzip/deflate (zlib), and can listen on a Unix domain socket. It is a library you embed in your own C++ process, not a drop-in for Go's net/http, so every handler has to be rewritten in C++.
how_it_is_fast: It runs on (Boost.)Asio. One acceptor thread gives each new socket to whichever of the N-1 per-thread io_contexts has the fewest live connections, so each connection's parse, route, handle and write cycle stays on one thread. Requests are parsed from a fixed 4 KB per-connection buffer by an embedded copy of the Node.js http_parser, a callback state machine derived from nginx's parser. Routing uses a per-method trie that is path-compressed at startup, and URL parameter types are fixed at compile time (black_magic::get_parameter_tag), so arguments go straight through strtoll/strtoull/strtod. Responses go out as a single scatter/gather write of asio buffers that point at the cached status line, each header name and value, and the body, with no header string building.
when_to_use: Adding a REST/JSON or WebSocket endpoint to an existing C++ application when you want Flask-style routes and URL parameters that are type-checked at compile time.

Short CPU-bound handlers on keep-alive HTTP/1.1, where per-request framework overhead dominates. That is the shape of the /json test where it beat TechEmpower's Go net/http code at every concurrency from 16 to 16,384.
Builds that want a header-only dependency (a single amalgamated header is available) needing only Asio headers, with OpenSSL and zlib opt-in.
Cross-platform services: CI builds GCC and Clang on Linux, Clang on macOS and MSVC on Windows; the docs list x86-64 and ARM64.
Serving behind a reverse proxy on a Unix domain socket (app.local_socket_path()).
when_not_to_use: Handlers that block on I/O (database calls, upstream HTTP). There are no native async handlers yet (README 'still in development', issue #258 open since 2021), and a blocking handler holds one of the hardware_concurrency()-1 worker threads.

You need HTTP/2 (issue #8, open since 2020), chunked responses (#1013 open) or streaming uploads. Request bodies are buffered whole into a std::string (#1064), and the parser path has no request-body size cap.

Very high connection counts. Open issue #791 reports 'Worker Crash: ... Transport endpoint is not connected' at 10,000 simultaneous connections, and file-descriptor exhaustion under floods only got accept back-off in v1.3.4 (#1188).

Internet-facing deployments that can't be kept current. v1.3.4 (2026-09-07) fixed five advisories, four rated high: a WebSocket global-middleware auth bypass, a WebSocket fragmented-payload limit bypass, JSON-depth stack overflow on Windows, and FileStore session path traversal.
You need a current, independent throughput figure. Crow is not in the TechEmpower rounds or in the-benchmarker's C++ set, and the Go comparison is from 2014.

integration.dependencies: Standalone Asio headers (docs: 1.28 to 1.30) or Boost.Asio (Boost >= 1.64 with CROW_USE_BOOST); optional OpenSSL (CROW_ENABLE_SSL) and zlib (CROW_ENABLE_COMPRESSION); pthreads
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (CMake sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17 and the setup docs require it, although the README still says 'modern C++ (11/14)'). The docs name g++ 9.4 and clang 10 as the CI compilers; CMake 3.15+ is needed only for install, tests or examples.
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 and ARM64 (docs), macOS (Clang, libc++/libstdc++) and Windows (MSVC) in CI; TCP or Unix domain sockets
integration.thread_safety: Handlers run concurrently on concurrency()-1 worker threads (multithreaded() = std::thread::hardware_concurrency()), and each connection is pinned to one thread, so any state shared between handlers needs your own locking. Finishing a crow::response from another thread is not supported: users report double-free crashes (#843) and async support is still open (#258). mustache::set_loader has a reported data race (#1246).

gotchas: The default log level is INFO, and at that level Crow logs a line for every request and every response. Call app.loglevel(crow::LogLevel::Warning) before measuring throughput.

Responses are written with a synchronous asio::write on the connection's worker thread (http_connection.h). A slow-reading client can therefore stall the other connections on that thread, and bodies above stream_threshold (1 MiB by default) are sent with the timeout timer cancelled.

In a 2024 report (#875, closed without a stated cause), a handler that added a header or returned crow::json fell to ~9.6k req/s at ~41 ms latency, versus ~335k req/s for a bare string. TCP_NODELAY is off unless you call app.tcp_nodelay(true) (available in v1.3.4), so benchmark your real handler both with and without it.

Current master sends no Date header: the code that wrote the per-thread cached Date is commented out in http_response.h. Add the header yourself if your clients or caches need it, and keep in mind that responses are a little lighter than those from servers that send Date, such as Go net/http.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Crow over Drogon or Oat++ when you want a header-only framework whose only required dependency is Asio, with Flask-style routes that are type-checked at compile time. Prefer Drogon or Oat++ when you need a current third-party comparison against Go net/http: both have 2026 the-benchmarker results, while Crow's comparison is a 2014 first-party run.
verified_claims_summary: Crow's original author ran a first-party test in October 2014 of the ipkn/crow code (submodule 3e5e91c, not today's CrowCpp/Crow) on TechEmpower's /json test, using an AWS c3.8xlarge with wrk on 8 cores. Crow did 136k-297k req/s against 93k-181k for TechEmpower's Go net/http code (GOMAXPROCS=NumCPU) at 16 to 16,384 connections, about 1.46x-1.64x, and was roughly level with Netty; the Go version, C++ compiler, flags and CPU model are not stated. A 2024 third-party run (Lemire, Crow 1.1.0, bombardier, 2x Xeon Gold 6338) measured 260k-380k req/s but included no Go baseline.
status_note: Actively maintained by the CrowCpp community fork: v1.3.4 shipped 2026-09-07, the last commit was 2026-09-23, and there are ~5.0k stars. The code is BSD-3-Clause (the logo and graphics are separately all-rights-reserved) and header-only, so it is easy to vendor, but pin v1.3.4 or later for the September 2026 security fixes.
